title: 1 · I want, I can
intro: Two little engine words, and you're building real sentences straight away. Say each answer out loud before you reveal it — the working-out is the part that sticks.

steps.teach: "Ik wil" = I want. Put the other verb on the end, unchanged. "komen" = to come (English come, c → k, plus the -en rule).
Any verb works the same way: "drinken" = to drink.
"Ik kan" = I can. Same shape: the second verb goes to the end.
To ask, just swap the first two words — exactly like English I can → can I.
"niet" = not. It goes after the bit it cancels, and before the verb at the end.
"je" = you (the everyday one). Swapped round for a question: "wil je".
steps.hint: Dutch has no "do" in questions — the verb just goes first.

steps.teach: Now put the two together.

title: 2 · I have, I am
intro: The two verbs you'll say more than any others — and one small habit of Dutch that catches English speakers out.

steps.teach: "Ik ben" = I am. "moe" = tired.
"Ik heb" = I have (say "hep" — a d or b at the end of a word hardens). "tijd" = time, straight from the long-i → ij rule.
Here's the habit: where English is hungry, Dutch has hunger. You own the feeling rather than being it.
steps.hint: Literally "I have hunger". Same for thirst: ik heb dorst.

steps.teach: "geen" = not a / no. Use it instead of "niet" when you're cancelling a plain noun.
No noun to cancel here, so it's niet again.
And the question is the same swap as before.

title: 3 · Ordering something
intro: Enough to walk into a café and be understood — and the one word that does the work of please, here you are, and go ahead.

steps.teach: "een" = a (say "un"). Add -je to make it a friendly, ordinary one: a "biertje" is just how you ask for a beer.
"alsjeblieft" = please — and also "here you are" when someone hands you something.
"Mag ik" = may I. The politest short way in.
"graag" = gladly. Drop it into "ik wil" and the demand becomes a request.
steps.hint: "broodje" is bread with -je on it — a roll, a sandwich.

steps.teach: On its own, "graag" is yes please.
"hoeveel" = how much (hoe + veel, how + many).
Literally thank-you-well. To a stranger you'd say dank u wel.

title: 4 · de, het, and -je
intro: Dutch has two words for "the" and no reliable way to tell which — except for one shortcut that always works.

steps.teach: Two words for "the": "de" and "het". Which one a noun takes is mostly something you pick up with the noun.
Most nouns take "de" — roughly two in three. When in doubt, guess de.
Here's the shortcut: anything ending in -je is always het. Always. No exceptions.
"een" = a, and it never changes — no de/het problem at all.
Plurals are all "de". The plural itself is usually -en; here the s softens to a z between vowels.
After -je the plural is just -s.

title: 5 · Talking about yesterday
intro: One pattern covers nearly all of the past in spoken Dutch: have + ge-something. It's the same shape as English "I have worked" — the Dutch just use it where English says "I worked".

steps.teach: Take the verb "werken", strip the -en, wrap it: ge- + werk + -t.
Same again with "maken": ge + maak + t. And Dutch says this where English says "I made".
Now "horen". This one ends in -d, not -t.
steps.hint: The ending is -t after a hard sound (t k f s ch p) and -d after everything else. Say both aloud — the -d one wants to be soft.

steps.teach: Some old everyday verbs go their own way, exactly like English eat/eaten. Worth simply knowing this one.
Verbs of being and going take "ben", not "heb" — like older English "I am come".
"gaan" = to go, "naar" = to. A movement, so "ben" again.
"niet" slots in before the ge- word at the end.

title: 6 · Already, still, not yet
intro: Four small words that carry most of the timing in everyday Dutch — and they sit in a place English doesn't expect.

steps.teach: "al" = already. "er" = there / here, the all-purpose little word for a place already understood.
"nog" = still.
"nog niet" = not yet. Literally still-not.
"niet meer" = not any more. Literally not-more.
In a question, "al" is the "yet".

steps.hint: nog niet, then the ge- word on the end.

steps.prompt: I don't want to any more.

title: 7 · Numbers, and the time
intro: Counting is nearly free — you already know most of it. Telling the time is not, because the Dutch look at the clock from the other side.

steps.teach: Say them out loud and the family likeness does the work.

steps.hint: five → vijf is the long-i → ij rule; six → zes is the s → z one.

steps.teach: Literally "how late is it?".
"uur" = hour. Say "ewr".
Here's the catch. Dutch half counts towards the next hour, not back from the last one. "Half acht" is half an hour before eight — half past seven.
steps.hint: Read it as half-way-to-eight and you'll never get it wrong.

steps.teach: "over" = past, "voor" = to. These two behave the way you expect.

title: 8 · Me, you, her, him
intro: The little words that make a sentence about somebody. Dutch keeps the same word whether the person is the object or comes after a preposition, which makes this simpler than it looks.

steps.teach: "me" = me. It doesn't change shape.
"je" = you, unstressed. "jou" when you want to lean on it.
"hem" = him.
"haar" = her — and it's also "her" as in her book. One word, both jobs.
"ons" = us.
And the possessives follow the owner, not the thing: "zijn" = his, "haar" = her.

title: 9 · Hij, zij, and the -in that isn't there
intro: Dutch marks people far less than its neighbours do. There's no masculine/feminine adjective agreement at all — which is a genuine relief, and worth knowing so you don't go looking for it.

steps.teach: "hij" = he, "zij" = she. "ze" is the everyday unstressed version of zij.
The verb doesn't change between them.
And here's the relief: adjectives don't change for the person either.
Job words mostly don't either — "arts" is a doctor of any gender.
steps.hint: no "a" before a job in Dutch

steps.teach: Where Dutch *does* have gender is in the articles — but it's de/het, which is about the word, not about people. "de" for most things, "het" for the rest.

steps.hint: het, and you simply have to learn which words take it

title: 10 · Asking without sounding blunt
intro: Dutch directness is real, but it isn't rudeness — there's a whole set of softeners, and they're small words rather than long constructions.

steps.teach: "Zou" = would. The politeness engine.
"Mag ik" = may I. Softer than "kan ik".
"even" makes any request sound like it takes two seconds.
"misschien" = maybe, and it softens anything it touches.
steps.answer: Zou je me misschien kunnen helpen?

steps.teach: "alsjeblieft" = please — and also "here you go" when handing something over.

title: 11 · Omdat, maar, hoewel
intro: The words that join two thoughts. One thing to watch: some of them send the verb to the end, and Dutch does this in exactly the places German does.

steps.teach: "maar" = but, and it changes nothing.
steps.prompt: I want to come, but I have no time
steps.answer: Ik wil komen, maar ik heb geen tijd.

steps.teach: "omdat" = because — and this one pushes the verb to the end of its half.
steps.hint: heb moves right to the end

steps.teach: Put it together and feel the verb slide back.
steps.prompt: I can't come because I have no time
steps.answer: Ik kan niet komen, omdat ik geen tijd heb.

steps.teach: "dat" = that, and it does the same thing.
"of" = whether, if.
steps.prompt: I don't know whether he's coming
steps.answer: Ik weet niet of hij komt.

steps.teach: "hoewel" = although.

steps.prompt: I'm coming although I have no time
steps.answer: Ik kom, hoewel ik geen tijd heb.

title: 12 · Even, maar, toch, hoor
intro: The small words that carry tone. None of them translate on their own, and they're the whole difference between correct Dutch and Dutch that sounds like a person.

steps.teach: "even" = just, briefly. It makes anything sound quick and unthreatening.
steps.prompt: I'll just pop to the shop
steps.answer: Ik moet even naar de winkel.

steps.teach: "maar" isn't only "but" — dropped into a request it means "go ahead".
"toch" contradicts gently — the "I did tell you" word.
steps.answer: Ik had het je toch gezegd.

steps.teach: "wel" is the opposite of niet, and it insists quietly.
"hoor" on the end is reassurance. It has no meaning at all and Dutch people say it constantly.
"hè?" on the end turns a statement into a check — like English "...right?".

title: 13 · Yesterday, and the verb at the end
intro: The Dutch past is built like the English one — have plus a done-word — with a single twist: the done-word goes to the very end of the sentence.

steps.teach: "hebben" + a past participle, exactly like English "I have eaten". "gegeten" = eaten.
And that's also the plain past. Dutch uses this for both "I have eaten" and "I ate".
Most past participles start with ge-. "gezegd" = said.
Now the twist. Add anything else and the participle still goes last.
steps.hint: gezegd stays at the very end

steps.teach: Verbs of going and becoming take "zijn" instead of hebben — like older English "I am come".
Same for worden, to become.

steps.answer: We zijn naar de bioscoop geweest.
